title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
formal: For every fixed real deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), do there exist constants \(C_\delta>0\) and \(a_\delta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that \[N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta n^{a_\delta}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge2?\] Here \(N_\delta(n)\), defined below, is the number of independent deletion traces needed to reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with success probability at least \(2/3\). Processing is unrestricted, and the length and deletion probability are known. Constants may depend on fixed \(\delta\).
definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.
why: Determine the intrinsic amount of information needed to recover an arbitrary string when repeated observations lose the positions of deleted symbols. This separates the statistical cost of hidden alignment from the computational cost of processing the observations.

progress.text: Chase proves the \(\Omega (n^{3/2}/\log ^{7} n)\) worst-case sample lower bound; preprint 2019, journal publication 2021.
Chase obtains \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces for arbitrary strings; preprint 2020 and STOC 2021 presentation.
Chen–De–Lee–Servedio establish nearly matching bounds for local statistical-query reconstruction, rather than unrestricted sample access.
Aamand–Liu–Narayanan obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) traces and polynomial time for mildly separated strings at sufficiently small constant deletion probability.
Burudgunte–Valiant–Wang prove an improved roughly \(n^{5}\) lower bound for the distinct circular trace model at ITCS.
Burudgunte–Valiant–Wang prove a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for general linear trace reconstruction, without a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm.
The graph-trace preprint separately retains the polynomial-to-quasipolynomial gap for ordinary binary strings; its new results concern graph degree sequences.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected July 2026 preprint gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for every fixed retention probability, while the unrestricted lower bound cited by it and the September graph-trace preprint remains polynomial. The cited quasipolynomial upper and polynomial lower bounds alone do not decide whether polynomially many traces suffice. Circular, local-SQ, separated-string and graph-trace results have different promises or observation models. No matching resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; source proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: The selected binary target asks whether a polynomial number of traces suffices for every fixed deletion rate. It does not require the optimal sample exponent or a polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its bound is \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\), for retention probability \(p=1-\delta\) and an absolute constant \(c\). This dated theorem does not by itself give a polynomial bound.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.
